overview: Pachyrhinosaurus ("thick-nosed lizard") was a large centrosaurine ceratopsid from the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian of Alberta and Alaska (~73–69 Ma), unusual for lacking a prominent nasal horn in adults — instead bearing a thick bony boss on the nose and a prominent frontal boss between the eyes. Three species are known, including P. perotorum from Alaska, which lived north of the Arctic Circle.

The Alaskan Pachyrhinosaurus population provides some of the best evidence that large dinosaurs could inhabit polar regions: the North Slope of Alaska was above the Arctic Circle at ~70 Ma, and Pachyrhinosaurus experienced months of polar darkness and cool temperatures, demonstrating that at least some dinosaurs could thrive in conditions far from the subtropical environments typically imagined.

fossilSites.name: Horseshoe Canyon Formation — Pipestone Creek
fossilSites.note: Early Maastrichtian bone bed with hundreds of Pachyrhinosaurus canadensis individuals — one of the largest ceratopsid bone beds known.

fossilSites.name: Prince Creek Formation

articles.title: Discovery and bone beds
articles.body: The Pipestone Creek bone bed near Grande Prairie, Alberta has yielded hundreds of Pachyrhinosaurus canadensis individuals — one of the richest centrosaurine accumulations known. Described by Langston in 1975, the genus has since grown to three species. The nasal boss (rather than a true horn) is the diagnostic feature: it grew throughout ontogeny and bore a keratinous covering in life.

articles.title: Arctic dinosaurs
articles.body: Pachyrhinosaurus perotorum from the North Slope of Alaska lived above 70° north latitude — within the Arctic Circle. Palaeogeographic reconstructions place this site at approximately the same polar position during the Late Cretaceous. The animals endured months of polar darkness and cool winters, contradicting the notion that non-avian dinosaurs were confined to warm tropical and subtropical environments.

articles.title: Boss function
articles.body: The thick flat nasal boss of Pachyrhinosaurus may have been used for intraspecific pushing contests — analogous to musk oxen head-butting — rather than the impaling function of a true nasal horn. The frill bore multiple accessory spikes and hooks that varied between species, serving display and species recognition functions.

record.description: Pachyrhinosaurus was a centrosaurine ceratopsid represented by three named North American species and large bonebeds. The type species P. canadensis was named from the St. Mary River Formation of Alberta, with referred material from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation, and bears a thick nasal boss rather than a conventional nasal horn.
facts: Bonebeds contain many disarticulated individuals and growth stages, not one herd frozen in behaviour.
Boss and frill ornament changed markedly during growth.
Migration and horn-covering shape are plausible but not directly demonstrated.

presentation.heroLead: A heavily built horned dinosaur that replaced its nose horn with a thick, flattened bony boss, known from dozens of skulls and rich bonebeds spanning three species in Alberta and Alaska.

animalParagraphs: Pachyrhinosaurus was a large, four-legged horned dinosaur of the centrosaurine group that lived in western North America during the last part of the Cretaceous. Adults were about six to eight metres long, with a deep body, a short tail and a heavy skull carrying a parrot-like beak and batteries of shearing teeth.

Instead of the nose horn seen in most ceratopsids, adult Pachyrhinosaurus grew a massive, flattened, rugose boss over the snout, with smaller bosses over the eyes. The frill carried a pair of long horns that curved upwards, plus a variable set of spikes and hooks along its rim; the three named species differ chiefly in the arrangement of these frill ornaments.

Because it is known from bonebeds containing many individuals of different sizes, the genus provides an unusually clear record of how the boss and frill developed as animals grew. Juveniles had small, horn-like nasal projections that were only later replaced by the thick boss. Whether the animals lived in large herds, and how the boss was used, are interpretations rather than direct observations.
animalHighlights: A thick, flattened nasal boss replaced the nose horn in adults, giving the genus its name, meaning "thick-nosed lizard".
Three named species, P. canadensis, P. lakustai and P. perotorum, differ mainly in the shape and arrangement of frill ornament.
Multi-individual bonebeds in Alberta and Alaska record growth from juvenile to adult in a single ceratopsid.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by beak and dental batteries
lifeCards.reason: The rostral beak and dental batteries with shearing wear facets are typical of ceratopsids that processed tough vegetation. No gut contents are known.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Limb and girdle bones from bonebeds show the robust, four-legged build shared by all ceratopsids. Walking speed and gait are modelled rather than observed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.level: Estimated from skulls and partial skeletons
lifeCards.reason: No single complete articulated adult skeleton is described; lengths and masses are scaled from skulls and disarticulated limb bones.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The shape of the boss and frill is directly known from many skulls, but the keratin covering of the boss, skin texture and colour are inferred.

locality.name: Scabby Butte
locality.note: Type locality of P. canadensis in the St. Mary River Formation. P. lakustai comes from the Pipestone Creek bonebed near Grande Prairie, Alberta, and P. perotorum from the Prince Creek Formation on the North Slope of Alaska.

presentation.classificationSummary: Pachyrhinosaurus is a centrosaurine ceratopsid and the name-bearer of the tribe Pachyrhinosaurini, a group of boss-bearing centrosaurines that also includes Achelousaurus. Its three species are consistently recovered as each other's closest relatives.

related.reason: Compare with a closely related, older boss-bearing centrosaurine from Montana.
Compare with a Montana centrosaurine that retained a forward-curving nasal horn.
Compare with a horn-bearing centrosaurine known from some of the largest bonebeds in Alberta.

questions.title: What covered the boss in life?
questions.copy: The rugose bone surface implies a keratinous covering, but its thickness and shape, whether a flat pad or a horn-like structure, cannot be read directly from the fossils.

questions.title: Did it migrate?
questions.copy: The presence of the genus in both Alberta and Arctic Alaska has prompted suggestions of seasonal migration, but bonebeds record where animals died, not where they travelled.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: Three species are named, but ornament changes with growth and varies between individuals, so some referrals of isolated skulls and bonebed material remain under study.

review.ageReviewNote: The genus-level range spans late Campanian P. lakustai through Maastrichtian P. canadensis and P. perotorum; species ages must not be merged.

evidence.summary: Pachyrhinosaurus was a centrosaurine ceratopsid represented by three named North American species and large bonebeds. The type species P. canadensis comes from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation and bears a thick nasal boss rather than a conventional nasal horn.

specimens.name: Holotype of P. canadensis
specimens.note: A partial skull from Scabby Butte, St. Mary River Formation, described by Sternberg in 1950; a second Scabby Butte skull, CMN 8866, was described alongside it.

specimens.name: Holotype of P. lakustai
specimens.institution: Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology, Drumheller
specimens.note: A skull from the Pipestone Creek bonebed, Wapiti Formation, near Grande Prairie; the bonebed has yielded hundreds of elements from many individuals.

specimens.name: Holotype of P. perotorum
specimens.institution: Perot Museum of Nature and Science, Dallas

panel.headline: Dozens of skulls and several bonebeds, spread across three species.
panel.standfirst: Pachyrhinosaurus is one of the better-sampled ceratopsids. Skulls of all growth stages and abundant disarticulated postcranial bones are known from bonebeds in Alberta and Alaska, although no single complete articulated skeleton has been described.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented across the bonebed material, but the postcranium is known mainly from disarticulated bones and individual skeletons are incomplete.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete and partial skulls of juveniles, subadults and adults, isolated frill and boss elements, and disarticulated vertebrae, ribs, girdle and limb bones from bonebeds at Scabby Butte and Pipestone Creek in Alberta and the Kikak-Tegoseak Quarry in Alaska.
knownRemains.note: Because bonebed material is disarticulated, most postcranial bones cannot be tied to particular skulls, and body proportions are reconstructed from mixed individuals.

media.caption: A Pachyrhinosaurus skull on display at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, Drumheller, Alberta. Display skulls may include restored sections; the thick nasal boss and frill horns are directly preserved features.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Numerous complete and partial skulls with nasal and supraorbital bosses, frills, beaks and dental batteries, spanning juvenile to adult growth stages.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae and ribs, known mainly as disarticulated bonebed elements.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapulae, coracoids, pelvic bones and fore- and hindlimb bones from bonebeds; articulated limbs are rare.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Bone histology has been sampled from bonebed material; no skin impressions, keratin or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: Pipestone Creek bonebed · P. lakustai
specimenCards.description: A dense bonebed near Grande Prairie that has yielded hundreds of elements, including skulls of several growth stages, and formed the basis of the 2008 monograph naming P. lakustai from holotype skull TMP 1986.55.258.
specimenCards.meta: Wapiti Formation · late Campanian · Royal Tyrrell Museum and Philip J. Currie Dinosaur Museum

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Skulls of many individuals showing the nasal boss and frill ornament at successive growth stages, plus abundant disarticulated postcranial bones from bonebeds.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: The bonebeds are read as mass-death assemblages of animals that lived in groups, and the boss as a display or combat structure that replaced the nasal horn during growth.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The form of the keratin covering on the boss, whether the animals migrated between Alberta and Alaska, the full postcranial anatomy of a single individual, and colour and skin texture.
